title: Film and Television
description: Ten reviews, interviews, profiles and essays about film and television: a quiet family film, a day on a TV set, a sound designer, the making of subtitles, an old drive-in theater, the habit of watching a whole series at once, a documentary maker, the makeup of a fantasy series, a science documentary and the money behind a film.

lessons.title: A Quiet Film Worth Waiting For
lessons.summary: A review of a gentle family film about two children, their grandmother and an old turtle.
lessons.text:
Now and then, a film arrives that asks nothing of its audience except patience. "The Turtle Summer," the second feature by the director Lena Hart, is such a film, and it rewards that patience.

The story is simple. After the death of their grandfather, two children, Maya and her younger brother Sam, spend a summer with their grandmother in a small house by a lake. Their parents are working in the city, and the grandmother, played gently by Ruth Calder, is not sure how to look after two children who seem to miss their phones more than their grandfather. What changes everything is a turtle. Early in the film, Sam finds an old turtle in the garden, and his grandmother tells him that it belonged to his grandfather, who fed it every morning for 40 years.

From that moment, the children have a job. They feed the turtle, build it a small pool and decorate its corner of the garden with stones and shells. While they decorate the garden, their grandmother begins, slowly, to tell them about the man they had hardly known.

Not once does the film raise its voice. The music is minimal: a piano, a few notes, and long periods of silence in which we hear only wind and water. The camera work is minimal too: Hart keeps the camera still, and a single conversation at the kitchen table can last 5 minutes. What the film understands is that sadness rarely speaks in speeches. It speaks in a sigh at the sink, or in a coat that nobody has moved from its hook. When the grandmother finally takes that coat down, her sigh says more than any line of dialogue could.

There are lovely images throughout. Butterflies gather over the flowers by the lake, and Maya draws every butterfly she sees. Later that summer, the grandfather's roses, which nobody has cared for, begin to bloom again, and the children watch them bloom with great pride. After a storm, a rainbow appears over the water, and the three of them stand outside without speaking. A weaker film would have added music to the rainbow; Hart simply lets us look.

The film's one unfortunate choice comes near the end. The family visits the cemetery, and the children leave a drawing of a butterfly on their grandfather's grave. The scene at the cemetery is beautiful. It is the long speech afterward, in which the grandmother explains what the turtle means, that is unfortunate, because it tells us what we had already understood.

Still, had the film been louder, it would have been easy to forget. At the end, the children go home happily, promising to come back next summer, and the turtle stays where it belongs, in the garden, as it has for 40 years.

Questions:
Who are the main characters of the film?
The main characters are two children, Maya and Sam, and their grandmother.
Why is the turtle important to the family?
It belonged to the children's grandfather, who fed it every morning for 40 years.
How do the children take care of the turtle?
They feed it, build it a small pool and decorate its corner of the garden with stones and shells.
What does the writer say about the music?
The music is minimal: a piano, a few notes and long periods of silence.
What does the writer think is unfortunate?
The long speech after the visit to the cemetery is unfortunate, because it explains what viewers had already understood.
How does the film end?
The children go home happily, and the turtle stays in the garden.

lessons.title: A Day on the Set of a Courtroom Drama
lessons.summary: A visitor spends a day on the set of a television drama and learns how much work goes into a few minutes on screen.
lessons.text:
At 6 in the morning, the parking lot outside an old factory on the edge of the city is already full. Inside, a team of 80 people is preparing to film a single scene of "Eastside Court," a television drama about a young prosecutor in a busy city court. I have been invited to spend a day on the set, and what strikes me first is how little of the day is spent filming.

The courtroom is not real. It was built inside the factory, and its layout copies a real one down to the smallest detail: the judge's seat at the front, the jury on the left, and the tables for the prosecution and the defense facing the judge. The only difference is that three of the walls can be removed, so that the cameras can move easily. Adjacent to the courtroom, behind a thin wall, is the office where the prosecutor and the rest of the prosecution team discuss their cases late at night. Because the two sets are adjacent, the crew can move between them in minutes.

Before anything can be filmed, there is the setup. Each new camera position needs a new setup: the lights are moved and the cameras are placed on their tracks. Victor Osei, who is in charge of the lights, tells me that a single setup can take an hour, while the moment it is used for may last less than a minute on screen. "People think we spend our days acting," he says. "Mostly, we spend them waiting."

Outside, a large generator sits in the parking lot. It powers the lights, which are far too strong for the factory's old electrical system. All morning, crew members haul heavy equipment from the trucks to the set on metal carts. One young assistant tells me that he hauls more cables in a day than he lifted in a year at his old office job.

In a corner, the costume department works at a long table covered with jewelry. Every piece of jewelry is photographed and recorded, because each accessory must look exactly the same in every shot. If the prosecutor wears a silver ring in the morning, she must wear the same ring when the scene continues after lunch. Grace Mills, who designs the costumes, explains that a missing accessory is a common mistake in television. "Not only do viewers notice a missing ring," she says, "but they write to us about it."

At about 2 in the afternoon, the actors finally arrive. The actress who plays the prosecutor takes her place at the prosecution's table, the director calls for silence, and the scene begins. It lasts 3 minutes. Then the director thanks everyone, an assistant pushes in a cart of coffee, and the crew begins a new setup.

By evening, the team has filmed 6 minutes of television. As I walk past the generator to my car, I understand that every minute on screen was built and carried there by dozens of people whom viewers will never see.

Questions:
What is "Eastside Court" about?
It is a television drama about a young prosecutor in a busy city court.
How is the layout of the courtroom set different from a real courtroom?
Three of its walls can be removed, so that the cameras can move easily.
What is a setup, and how long can it take?
A setup is the preparation for each new camera position, and a single setup can take an hour.
Why does the costume department record every piece of jewelry?
Each accessory must look exactly the same in every shot.

lessons.title: Listening Closely: An Interview with a Sound Designer
lessons.summary: A sound designer explains where the sounds of a film come from and how he builds them.
lessons.text:
Tomas Reyes has designed the sound for more than 30 films, including the space drama "Silent Orbit" and the family film "Little Giant." We met in his studio, a small room full of recording equipment, old records and, rather unusually, fruit.

What does a sound designer actually do?

Most of what you hear in a film was not recorded on the day it was filmed. The actors' voices usually are, but almost everything else is added later: steps, doors, wind, rain. My job is to decide what the world of a film sounds like, and then to build that world, one sound at a time.

Where do all these sounds originate?

They originate in all kinds of places. Many come from collections that anyone can buy, but I try not to use those, because they are generic. A generic door sounds like every door in every film. I want the door in my film to sound like that particular door, in that particular house.

And the fruit?

For "Little Giant," we needed the sound of a giant walking through a forest, so we recorded ourselves stepping on boxes of berries. The berries gave each step a wet, soft texture. A sound has a texture, just as a coat does: it can be rough or smooth, wet or dry. What I listen for, before anything else, is texture.

What else do you use?

Towels, mostly. A wet towel, hit hard against a table, makes a very good sound for a fight. A dry towel, moved slowly, sounds like wind through grass.

How did you make the giant's voice?

The giant has a mighty voice, so we recorded my own voice and slowed it down until it was deep enough. Then we added the sound of a lion, very quietly.

So you manipulate recordings a great deal.

Yes. Rarely do I use a sound exactly as it was recorded. I manipulate almost everything: I slow it down, I change its pitch, I mix it with other sounds. However, I almost never use synthetic sounds, which are created entirely by a computer. Synthetic sounds can be wonderful in a space film, and in "Silent Orbit" much of the ship is synthetic. But even there, I mixed in a recording of an old kitchen fan, because a sound with nothing real in it tends to feel cold.

Is there one sound you are especially proud of?

A very small one. In "Little Giant," an old man plays a record for his wife. We recorded more than 20 different needles before we found the right one. The needle had to sound tired, like the man.

Do you ever get tired of listening?

I take an occasional day off. Apart from that, and the occasional complaint from my family about wet towels on the kitchen table, I am happy to listen all the time.

Questions:
Why does Tomas Reyes try not to use generic sounds?
A generic door sounds like every door in every film, and he wants each sound to fit its own place.
What did the berries give to the giant's steps?
They gave each step a wet, soft texture.
How did he make the giant's mighty voice?
He recorded his own voice, slowed it down and quietly added the sound of a lion.
Why does he almost never use synthetic sounds?
He feels that a sound with nothing real in it tends to feel cold.
Why did he record more than 20 needles?
The needle had to sound tired, like the old man in the scene.

lessons.title: Between the Lines: How Subtitles Are Made
lessons.summary: An overview of how a translator turns spoken dialogue into short lines of text on the screen.
lessons.text:
Most viewers never think about subtitles unless they are bad. When they are good, we forget that someone wrote every line. For hundreds of films and series, that someone has been Hana Mori, who has done this work for 15 years. What follows is a short overview of her method.

The first step is to watch the whole film without writing anything. "I need an overview before I start," Mori says. "If I don't know how a story ends, I can't know which words matter at the beginning." Only after this first viewing does she open the script.

The second step is timing. Each line must appear when a character starts speaking and disappear when the speech ends, and every timing is adjusted by hand, often frame by frame. Even after the timing has been adjusted once, Mori watches the film again and checks it a second time.

The hardest part, however, is cutting. People speak much faster than most viewers can read, so there is usually room for two short lines, and sometimes for only a handful of words. Reading, Mori points out, is cognitive work. A viewer who is reading cannot fully watch, and if the text is excessive, the cognitive effort becomes so great that the viewer stops watching the film and only reads it. "Excessive text is the most common mistake," she says. "People who are new to the job have a tendency to translate every word. It's a natural tendency, because every word feels important. But a handful of well-chosen words is worth more than a full sentence that nobody has time to read."

Another difficulty is that a film is linear. A reader of a book can go back and read a sentence again, but a viewer in a theater cannot. Because the experience is linear, each line must be clear on first reading.

Then there is tone. When a character is rude, Mori must decide how rude the translation should be. "It is easy to be diplomatic," she says, "and to make people sound nicer than they are. But a diplomatic translation of an angry man is a bad translation." Jokes are harder still. The chances that a joke survives word for word in another language are slim, and the chances that viewers will laugh at a joke they have to think about are even slimmer, so she often writes a new joke that works in the same way.

Finally, there is uncertainty. Sometimes a line is spoken too quietly to hear, or the script and the film do not match. In moments of uncertainty, she writes to the studio and waits for an answer, even if it costs her a day.

If she had not learned to cut, she says, she would not be doing this job today.

Questions:
Why does Hana Mori watch the whole film before she starts writing?
She needs an overview, because she has to know how the story ends to know which words matter.
Why is excessive text a problem?
Reading is cognitive work, and with excessive text the viewer stops watching and only reads.
What does it mean that a film is linear?
It means that a viewer cannot go back, so each line must be clear on first reading.
Why does she not want to be too diplomatic?
A diplomatic translation of an angry man is a bad translation.
What does she do in moments of uncertainty?
She writes to the studio and waits for an answer.

lessons.title: The Starlight Drive-In
lessons.summary: A writer returns to the old drive-in theater of her childhood and finds it still open.
lessons.text:
When I was a child, the Starlight Drive-In was the center of summer. It stands on a flat piece of land outside a small town in the southwest, with the desert on three sides and a highway on the fourth. On Friday nights, my father drove us there in his old car, parked in the third row, and let my sister and me sit on the roof until the film began.

Last month, after almost 30 years, I drove back to see whether the Starlight was still there. It is. The screen is the same tall white wall, a little gray now, and the sign at the entrance still shows a star with one broken light.

The man at the entrance is Frank Ortiz, who has owned the drive-in since 1985. He calls himself its keeper, rather than its owner. "You don't own a place like this," he told me. "You keep it going for the next person." As its keeper, he repairs the equipment himself, paints the screen every spring, and sweeps the lot every Sunday morning.

Much of that equipment is antique. The speakers that hang on car windows date from 1962, although most visitors now listen through their car radios. The ticket booth is antique too, a small wooden box with a window that sticks. Frank's wife, Rosa, sells drinks and cookies that she bakes herself. Her cookies, I am happy to report, are exactly as good as I remembered.

Nowadays, most people watch films on their phones or on large screens at home, and Frank knows it. "Nowadays, nobody needs to come here," he said. "So the people who come really want to." For decades, the drive-in was the town's main form of recreation, along with the swimming pool and the baseball field. Today it is one form of recreation among many, but on a summer weekend it is still full.

That night, Frank showed an old football film, a favorite with the regulars. It is a simple story about a small-town team, and every time the team scored a touchdown, people in the cars sounded their horns and flashed their lights. By the final touchdown, the whole lot was shining like a city.

As the night grew cold, I turned up the collar of my jacket, the way my father always did. He used to sit with his collar up and his arms crossed, laughing at every joke. I realized that I was sitting exactly as he had sat.

At home, I keep an old receipt in a book on my shelf. It is from the Starlight, dated 1994: two tickets, one popcorn, $6 in total. On my way out last month, Frank gave me a new receipt for my ticket, and I put it in the same book, next to the old one.

Questions:
Where is the Starlight Drive-In?
It is outside a small town in the southwest, with the desert on three sides and a highway on the fourth.
Why does Frank Ortiz call himself the keeper of the drive-in?
He believes that you do not own a place like this; you keep it going for the next person.
What antique things are still at the drive-in?
The speakers that hang on car windows and the small wooden ticket booth are antique.
What did people do every time the team scored a touchdown?
They sounded their horns and flashed their lights.
What does the writer keep in a book at home?
The writer keeps an old receipt from 1994 and a new receipt from her last visit.

lessons.title: One More Episode
lessons.summary: A columnist weighs the pleasures and the costs of watching a whole series in a few days.
lessons.text:
A generation ago, people sat in front of the television and surfed the channels, hoping to find something worth watching. If nothing was on, they went to bed. Nowadays, nobody needs to surf anything. A whole series waits for us on a screen, and when one episode ends, the next begins after a few seconds, unless we stop it. Many of us do not.

Watching a whole season in a weekend has become so ordinary that people speak about it openly. A colleague of mine openly admits that she watched 10 episodes of a crime series in one Saturday. Ten years ago, she might have kept that to herself. So is this a harmless pleasure or a bad habit? I want to weigh both sides fairly, and I promise not to preach, since I am as guilty as anyone.

The case in favor is strong. Many series today are written to be watched this way. Their stories are long and connected, and they are more entertaining when the details are fresh in your mind than when you wait a week and forget who is who. Watching together can also be social: friends who watch the same series at the same time talk about it, argue about it and share it. For hardcore fans, finishing a new season on the weekend it appears is part of the fun. And for a tired person at the end of a hard week, a few hours of entertaining television may be exactly what is needed.

The case against is just as strong. The services that offer these series count their subscribers in millions, and every subscriber who keeps watching is worth money to them. Not only does the next episode start by itself, but our phones receive a notification whenever a new season appears. A notification arrives, and an evening disappears. The problem is not that the shows are bad; it is that they are designed to be hard to stop. Sleep is usually the first thing we lose, followed by time with family, reading and exercise.

What, then, should we do? I do not think we need to discontinue our subscriptions, although one friend of mine did discontinue hers for a month and said she slept better than she had in years. What we need is to regulate the habit, rather than to give it up. Some people regulate it with a simple rule: no more than two episodes on a weeknight. Even hardcore fans can live with a rule like that. Others turn off every notification, so that the services cannot choose the evening for them.

Had I made such a rule a year ago, I would be less tired today. But I am not here to preach. A good story, watched with pleasure, is one of the joys of modern life. The trick is to make sure that we are the ones deciding when it ends.

Questions:
What did people do with the television a generation ago?
They surfed the channels, hoping to find something worth watching.
Why are many series more entertaining when watched in a few days?
Their stories are long and connected, and the details are fresh in your mind.
Why are subscribers important to the services?
Every subscriber who keeps watching is worth money to them.
How do notifications affect our evenings?
A notification arrives when a new season appears, and an evening can disappear.
How does the writer suggest that people regulate the habit?
They can allow themselves no more than two episodes on a weeknight, or turn off every notification.

lessons.title: The People Next Door: A Documentary Maker
lessons.summary: A profile of a documentary maker who films ordinary communities and shows her films locally first.
lessons.text:
Elena Vargas has made five documentaries in 12 years, and not one of them has been about a famous person. Her subjects are shepherds, bus drivers, nurses, and the people of small towns. "Famous people have enough cameras," she says. "I'm interested in the people standing behind them."

Vargas grew up in a small town in the north. Her father was a builder, and as a child she often went with him to work, watching houses rise from empty ground. "A builder doesn't start with the roof," she says. "He starts with the ground and works upward, slowly. A documentary is the same."

She studied journalism at a state university, planning to write for a newspaper. It was in her last semester that everything changed. That semester, she took a film class taught by Daniel Brooks, an older documentary maker who became her mentor. Brooks gave her a camera for the weekend and told her to film something she did not understand. She filmed her town's market, and when she watched the material, she realized that she wanted to make films, not write articles. "Journalism taught me to ask questions," she says. "My mentor taught me to wait for the answers."

A month after her graduation, she spent a whole year with a family of shepherds in the mountains. The result, "High Pasture," follows one shepherd and his daughter as they move their sheep from the valley to the summer fields. We see the shepherd checking each animal, the daughter learning the paths, and the weather changing over the mountains.

Her second film was about an electoral campaign in a town of 3,000 people, where two people from the same street, a teacher and a shop owner, competed to become mayor. Vargas filmed both sides equally. What interested her was not politics but behavior: how people who disagreed during the electoral campaign continued to live side by side after it ended.

Her most recent film, "After the Water," shows a town rebuilding after a flood. It is a film about solidarity. Builders from nearby towns came to help for free, families shared their homes, and the school became a kitchen for everyone. Vargas filmed this solidarity without music or comment, allowing the people to speak for themselves.

She always shows her films locally first. Before any festival sees them, they are shown in a school hall in the town, to the people who appear in them. "If my film isn't true for them, it isn't true," she says. Only after the local showing does she send the film anywhere else.

Questions:
What did Elena Vargas learn from her father, the builder?
She learned to start with the ground and work upward slowly, which she says is like making a documentary.
What happened in her last semester of journalism school?
She took a film class with Daniel Brooks, who became her mentor, and she realized she wanted to make films.
What did she do after her graduation?
She spent a year with a family of shepherds in the mountains and made a film about them.
What interested her about the electoral campaign?
She was interested in how people who disagreed continued to live side by side after the campaign.
How did people show solidarity after the flood?
Builders came to help for free, families shared their homes, and the school became a kitchen for everyone.
Why does she show her films locally first?
She believes that if a film is not true for the people in it, it is not true.

lessons.title: The Faces of Wizard Hollow
lessons.summary: A profile of the makeup artist who creates the troll, the wizard and the other faces of a children's fantasy series.
lessons.text:
Every Saturday morning, about 2 million children watch "Wizard Hollow," a fantasy series about a young wizard named Pip who lives in a village at the edge of a dark forest. Few of them know the name Clara Fenn, but they know her work. It is Fenn, the head of makeup for the series, who turns ordinary actors into wizards, trolls and talking animals.

Her most famous creation is Grumble, a troll who lives under the village bridge. In the first season, Grumble was meant to be frightening, a troll who wanted to conquer the village and take its children's toys. But young viewers loved him from the start, and by the second season the troll had become the darling of the show. Today Grumble is a gentle giant who wants to conquer nothing more than his fear of the dark.

Creating the troll's face takes 3 hours every morning. The actor sits in a chair while Fenn and two assistants attach large pieces of soft rubber to his face, neck and hands. The difficulty is not making him look like a troll; it is making sure he can still act. "Children read facial expressions better than adults do," Fenn explains. "If the rubber is too thick, the actor's facial movements disappear, and the troll stops feeling alive." For this reason, the pieces around the eyes and mouth are as thin as paper.

The wizards are easier. Pip wears only a little makeup, but his teacher, the old wizard Moss, needs a long white beard, deep lines on his face, and a staff with a green gem at the top. The gem is made of glass, and inside it a tiny light is controlled by a member of the crew. When the gem glows, the audience knows that magic is about to happen.

There is also a prophet. Old Wren, who lives on a hill above the village, is the prophet of Wizard Hollow, although her predictions are usually wrong, which is one of the show's running jokes. Fenn gave the prophet silver paint around the eyes, so that she always seems to be looking at something far away.

Before any new makeup is used on an actor, it must be tested, and Fenn's brother has been her guinea pig for 20 years. "He has been a troll, a wolf and a tree," she says, laughing. "Being my guinea pig is not an easy job." Pip, by the way, also has a pet guinea pig, which needs no makeup at all.

What keeps Fenn interested after so many seasons? She calls it the eternal question of her work: how far can a face change before it stops being human? "It's an eternal question," she says, "and every new character gives me a different answer."

Questions:
What is "Wizard Hollow" about?
It is about a young wizard named Pip who lives in a village at the edge of a dark forest.
How did Grumble the troll change after the first season?
He became the darling of the show, a gentle giant who wants to conquer only his fear of the dark.
Why must the rubber around the troll's eyes and mouth be very thin?
Children read facial expressions well, and thick rubber would hide the actor's facial movements.
What happens when the gem on the wizard's staff glows?
The audience knows that magic is about to happen.
Who has been Clara Fenn's guinea pig for 20 years?
Her brother has been her guinea pig for 20 years.

lessons.title: Stones That Remember
lessons.summary: A review of a science documentary that follows researchers who study fossils.
lessons.text:
Science documentaries often try too hard. They fill the screen with bright graphics and loud music, as if the audience might leave at any moment. "Stones That Remember," a new series in four parts, has the confidence to do the opposite. It shows us people at work, explains what they are doing, and trusts us to find it as interesting as they do. Rarely have I watched a documentary that made patience look so exciting.

The first episode begins in a dry river valley, where a team of researchers is looking for fossils. A fossil, the narrator reminds us, is what remains when a living thing is slowly turned to stone over millions of years. For 10 minutes we simply watch the team walk, look and walk again. Then one of them, a young researcher named Ama Boateng, finds a small, dark object in the sand. It is a tooth. From a single tooth, she explains, a scientist can tell what an animal ate, how old it was and sometimes how it died.

What follows is the best part of the series. Back in the laboratory, the fossil is cleaned with dental tools, the same small picks and brushes that a dentist uses. Boateng says that dental tools are perfect for the work because they are fine enough to remove sand without damaging the stone. The camera stays close to her hands for several minutes, and the only sound is the quiet scratching of metal on rock.

In the second episode, the team takes the tooth to a molecular laboratory, where scientists study the fossil at the level of the molecule. Inside some fossils, it turns out, a few original molecules survive for millions of years, and these can show how the animal is related to animals living today. The series explains this molecular work clearly, with one simple drawing of a molecule.

The third episode is the most beautiful. The team descends into a cave, where the walls are full of fossils of sea creatures, proof that the land was once under water. As they descend, the only light comes from their helmets, and the walls seem to move around them. Later, in the laboratory, the filmmakers place a fossil on a small table and slowly rotate it, so that we see every side. Watching the fossil rotate in silence, I understood why the researchers love their work.

The final episode repeats too much of what came before, but that is a minor complaint. If I had seen this series as a teenager, I might be a scientist today. It is the kind of documentary that can inspire young viewers, and, I suspect, it will inspire a few older ones too.

Questions:
What is a fossil, according to the narrator?
A fossil is what remains when a living thing is slowly turned to stone over millions of years.
What can a scientist learn from a single tooth?
A scientist can tell what an animal ate, how old it was and sometimes how it died.
Why are dental tools used to clean the fossil?
They are fine enough to remove sand without damaging the stone.
What happens in the molecular laboratory?
Scientists study the fossil at the level of the molecule to find out how the animal is related to animals living today.
Why do the filmmakers rotate the fossil on a small table?
They rotate it so that viewers can see every side.
Whom does the writer think the series will inspire?
It will inspire young viewers and probably a few older ones too.

lessons.title: Follow the Money: Who Pays for a Film?
lessons.summary: An economist explains in an interview where the money for an independent film comes from.
lessons.text:
Nina Okoro is an economist who studies the film industry. She advises young directors on how to pay for their work. We asked her to explain where the money for a film really comes from.

Why does the film industry need an economist?

Because films are very expensive, and nobody knows in advance which ones will succeed. An economist studies how people make decisions when they cannot be sure of the result, and that describes film better than almost any other business.

Let's start with the large studios. Who pays for their films?

The largest studios are owned by companies with thousands of shareholders. Each shareholder owns a small part of the company and expects it to make a profit. This is why big studios prefer familiar stories: a shareholder would rather see a safe profit than an interesting risk.

And independent filmmakers?

They put the money together from many small sources. A typical independent film might be paid for by a public film fund, a few private investors and a television channel that buys the right to show it later. Often a broker is involved as well. A broker sells the right to show the film in other countries before it is even made, and that money helps pay for the filming.

How important are public film funds?

Very important. For many small films, a grant from a public fund is the first injection of money, and that first injection persuades everyone else to join. Each fund receives many more applications than it can support, so every applicant must prepare a script, a budget and a plan for reaching an audience.

What should an applicant do to impress a fund?

The applicants who impress a fund most are not always the ones with the best scripts. What impresses a fund is a clear plan: who will watch the film, and how they will find it. Before applying, every applicant should ask for a consultation. Most funds offer a free consultation to first-time filmmakers, and a single hour with an advisor can save months of work.

What is the biggest danger for a small production?

Costs that grow faster than the money. Rising costs can choke a small production long before it is finished. I have seen good films choke because the team spent half its money in the first two weeks of filming. Had they planned more carefully, those films would be in theaters now.

Finally, is it still possible to make a film without much money?

Absolutely. Never has it been cheaper to film and edit a story. The difficult part is no longer making a film; it is getting people to watch it.

Questions:
Why does the film industry need an economist, according to Nina Okoro?
Films are very expensive, and nobody knows in advance which ones will succeed.
Why do big studios prefer familiar stories?
Their shareholders expect a profit and would rather see a safe profit than an interesting risk.
What does a broker do for an independent film?
A broker sells the right to show the film in other countries before it is made.
What impresses a fund most?
A clear plan for who will watch the film and how they will find it impresses a fund most.
Why should every applicant ask for a consultation?
A single hour with an advisor can save months of work.
How can rising costs choke a small production?
They can grow faster than the money, so the production cannot be finished.
